strengths: The paper addresses a useful control problem: specifying an interaction target with a first-frame mask and text, without requiring trajectories or dense motion guidance. The proposed modification is simple and practical.

Target-alignment improvements are substantial. Compared with CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, contact score increases from 0.692 to 0.896 and human-evaluated interaction accuracy from 0.596 to 0.892. Pairwise human preferences also favor the proposed method.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence for the attention loss: removing it reduces contact score to 0.688. Additional experiments support selecting semantically relevant blocks and supervising video-to-text attention.

The supplement provides useful training and inference details, including LoRA configuration, optimization settings, selected blocks, and computational cost. Qualitative examples illustrate same-category target selection and potential transfer to non-human actors.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate. Mask-channel conditioning, token-associated attention supervision, and semantic block selection build closely on established diffusion-control techniques. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its claimed novel loss from prior spatial attention guidance or establish that the contribution extends beyond an effective task-specific combination.

Evaluation is limited to 50 images on one backbone. Benchmark provenance, separation from training scenes and subjects, and action/object coverage are insufficiently documented. There are no uncertainty estimates or quantitative breakdowns for unseen categories, multiple identical objects, or changing the target mask while holding the image and prompt fixed.

The contact metric measures any detected hand-contact region overlapping the initial target mask in at least one frame. This does not establish completion of the requested action, sustained interaction, or physical plausibility; object movement can also invalidate the fixed spatial reference. Human studies strengthen the evidence for target alignment, but their questions do not explicitly assess action completion or physical correctness.

Comparative evidence remains narrow. The same-data baseline is valuable, but the principal spatial-control competitor is an adapted inference-time attention-modulation method. Drag-based comparisons are qualitative and use coarse controls. Stronger matched-input spatial-conditioning baselines would help establish the specific advantage of the proposed supervision.

The claim that video quality is not compromised is too strong. Table 1 reports motion smoothness of 0.905 versus 0.990 for the same-data baseline, with average quality also slightly lower. The paper should acknowledge and investigate this targeting–quality tradeoff rather than relying on the aggregate score.

The 3D HOI application does not substantiate the stronger planning and physical-interaction claims. Appendix A.2 states that object-motion modules are disabled and resulting human motions are manually aligned with the scene. Without quantitative contact, penetration, task-success, or baseline evaluations, this demonstrates a preliminary human-motion imitation pipeline rather than validated zero-shot physical HOI.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful control problem: specifying which object an actor should interact with using only an initial-frame mask and an action prompt, without requiring motion trajectories.

The reported target-alignment improvements are substantial. Compared with CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, contact score increases from 0.692 to 0.896 and human-evaluated interaction accuracy from 0.596 to 0.892. The human studies provide evidence beyond the automatic metric.

The ablations meaningfully support the proposed mechanism. Removing the attention loss reduces contact score to 0.688, while experiments on block selection, attention direction, and loss weight help explain the final design.

The approach is straightforward to implement, and the supplement provides useful training and inference details, including LoRA configuration, selected blocks, optimization settings, and computational cost.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently established relative to prior spatial attention guidance. The main ingredients are mask concatenation, supervision of a target token's attention, and empirical selection of attention blocks. A stronger comparison with existing attention-grounding objectives or alternative mask-conditioning architectures is needed to establish the distinctive contribution.

The evaluation covers only 50 images with five generations each and one backbone. Dataset provenance, separation from the 1,290 training clips, and the validation protocol for selecting blocks and hyperparameters are not sufficiently documented. There are no confidence intervals or quantitative breakdowns by action, target size, or scene complexity.

The contact metric is an incomplete proxy for successful interaction: it accepts any detected hand-object contact overlapping the initial target mask in any frame. It does not verify action completion, persistent object identity, or physical plausibility, and a fixed mask is problematic when objects move. Hand contact also does not adequately evaluate actions such as sitting. Human evaluation mitigates this concern but does not establish these broader capabilities.

The claim that video quality is preserved is too strong. Table 1 reports motion smoothness falling from 0.990 for the data-fine-tuned baseline to 0.905, with average quality decreasing from 0.818 to 0.812. The paper should investigate and acknowledge this tradeoff rather than relying on the aggregate score.

Baseline coverage remains narrow: quantitative comparisons largely involve the same backbone and one adapted inference-time attention method. The qualitative drag comparisons use coarse controls and do not establish superiority over stronger task-adapted conditioning methods. A quantitative counterfactual test that changes only the target mask among identical objects would more directly establish controllability.

The downstream 3D HOI and robotics claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Appendix A.2 states that object-motion modules are disabled and reconstructed motions are manually aligned with the scene. Without quantitative interaction success, object dynamics, collision measurements, or comparisons, these demonstrations support human-motion imitation rather than validated physical human-object interaction or robotic planning.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful control problem: generating interactions with a specific object using only its initial-frame mask and a text prompt. This interface avoids the substantial effort required to specify motion trajectories or dense temporal guidance.

The central result is convincing within the reported benchmark. Compared with CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, contact accuracy improves from 0.692 to 0.896 and human-rated interaction accuracy from 0.596 to 0.892. Pairwise preferences also favor the proposed method, providing evidence beyond the automatic metric.

The ablations meaningfully isolate the proposed mechanism. Mask conditioning without attention supervision achieves only 0.688 contact accuracy; experiments additionally support selecting semantic blocks and supervising video-to-text attention.

The approach is practical and reasonably well specified. The supplement provides the backbone, LoRA configuration, optimizer, training schedule, selected blocks, inference settings, and computational costs. Qualitative examples demonstrate promising target selection and transfer beyond human interactions.
weaknesses: The evaluation is small and insufficiently characterized: 50 images with five generations each, without clear benchmark provenance, comprehensive train/test separation details, category breakdowns, or uncertainty estimates. Quantitative counterfactual tests that change only the target mask would more directly establish reliable instance-level control.

Contact Score measures detected hand-contact overlap with the initial target mask in any frame. It does not establish completion of the requested action, sustained physical interaction, or target identity after object movement, and is unsuitable for some demonstrated interactions such as sitting. Human evaluations mitigate this concern but primarily assess target interaction rather than full action correctness.

The claim that video quality is preserved needs qualification. Motion smoothness falls from 0.990 for the data-matched baseline to 0.905, while average video quality decreases from 0.818 to 0.812. The paper should investigate this tradeoff instead of asserting that quality is unaffected.

The technical novelty is incremental relative to existing spatial conditioning and attention-guidance methods. Data-matched and mask-only baselines are valuable, but comparisons with alternative learned spatial-conditioning approaches would strengthen the evidence. Qualitative drag-method comparisons do not establish broad superiority over controllable video generation methods.

The downstream 3D HOI and robotics implications exceed the demonstrated evidence. The supplement states that object-motion modules are disabled and generated motions are manually aligned with the scene. Without object dynamics, interaction-success measurements, or physical-validity comparisons, these results demonstrate a preliminary motion-imitation pipeline rather than validated physical interaction planning.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful control problem: specifying which object an actor should interact with using only an initial-frame mask and an action prompt, without requiring a predefined motion trajectory.

The central empirical improvement is substantial. Against CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, Contact Score improves from 0.638 to 0.878 and human-rated interaction accuracy from 0.596 to 0.892. Human preferences provide complementary evidence beyond the automatic detector.

The ablations meaningfully isolate the proposed supervision: mask conditioning without attention loss achieves only 0.647 Contact Score. Experiments also examine attention direction, block selection, loss weight, mask perturbations, and noisy captions.

The supplementary evaluation strengthens the main result: gains persist under consecutive-frame contact requirements and a contact-plus-motion metric. These results reduce concerns that the improvement depends entirely on single-frame contact.

The implementation is relatively lightweight and reasonably documented, including LoRA configuration, optimization settings, training cost, and inference time. Qualitative examples demonstrate promising flexibility across targets, actions, and non-human actors.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: additional mask conditioning, token-to-region attention alignment, and semantic block selection build on established diffusion-control ideas. The strongest contribution is their effective application to interaction targeting; positioning against prior spatial-grounding and attention-supervision methods should be sharper.

Evaluation covers only 80 initial images and one backbone. The manuscript does not adequately document benchmark image provenance, dataset composition, or systematic separation from training scenes and subjects. Confidence intervals and variability across independent training runs are absent, particularly weakening conclusions about the smaller block-selection improvements.

The automatic metrics remain imperfect proxies for successful interaction. Contact is evaluated against the initial target mask rather than a tracked object identity, and the detector primarily recognizes human-hand contacts. Consecutive-frame overlap and target displacement do not establish completion of the requested action or physical correctness. Human studies mitigate this concern but do not fully validate these broader claims.

Comparisons establish an advantage over the base model, same-data fine-tuning, and an adapted attention-modulation baseline, but do not establish competitiveness against stronger contemporary video backbones or alternative learned spatial-conditioning methods. The attention-baseline reporting also needs reconciliation: Table 10 includes a 0.613 configuration, whereas Table 1 reports 0.546, using different sampling counts.

The claims about physically plausible 3D HOI and motion planning exceed the demonstrated evidence. Appendix A.2 disables object-motion modules and manually aligns simulated human motion with the scene. There are no quantitative interaction-success, collision, object-dynamics, or control evaluations. This supports a preliminary motion-imitation demonstration rather than validated physical interaction planning.

Some reporting claims need qualification. Motion smoothness decreases from 0.990 for same-data fine-tuning to 0.937, despite the claim that generation quality is uncompromised. Block selection is also inconsistent: Section 4.3 specifies every fifth block, while Appendix A.1 specifies every third block, consistent with the seven-block ablation.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful control problem: generating interactions with a specified existing object using only an initial-frame mask and an action prompt, without requiring a prescribed motion trajectory.

The core contribution has substantial empirical support. Compared with CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, Contact Score improves from 0.638 to 0.878 and human-rated interaction accuracy improves from 0.596 to 0.892. Human preferences also favor the proposed method, providing evidence beyond the automatic detector.

The ablations meaningfully isolate the attention loss: mask conditioning without that loss achieves only 0.647 Contact Score. Additional experiments examine attention direction, block selection, loss weight, mask perturbations, and caption quality.

The appendix strengthens the evaluation with consecutive-frame contact and target-motion metrics, which preserve the method's substantial advantage. Training and inference settings are reasonably detailed, and the limitations are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental. Mask concatenation, a designated text token, and attention-to-mask supervision build on established spatial-conditioning ideas. The paper should more precisely distinguish its learning objective from prior attention-grounding methods; its strongest contribution is their effective application to interaction generation.

The benchmark contains only 80 initial images, and its image provenance, selection procedure, and separation from training scenes and subjects are insufficiently documented. Five generations per image do not provide 400 independent scene-level tests. Confidence intervals, scene-level variability, and human-study agreement are not reported.

Contact Score measures overlap with the target's initial mask, rather than persistent object identity or successful execution of the requested action. The extended metrics help but retain this spatial limitation, and target displacement can reflect camera motion or tracking errors. The human studies mitigate these concerns, but neither establishes detailed action correctness or physical plausibility.

Baseline coverage remains limited to one backbone and an adapted attention-modulation method. The latter is not fully convincing: Table 10 contains a configuration scoring 0.613, whereas Table 1 reports 0.546 under a different sampling protocol, without clearly explaining configuration selection. Equation 7 also appears to assign negative infinity to unrelated attention entries unless its scope is restricted, making the adaptation difficult to verify.

The downstream physical-interaction claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Appendix A.2 explicitly disables object-motion modules in PhysHOI and manually aligns the resulting human motion with the scene. This supports a human-motion imitation demonstration, but does not establish physically correct human-object interaction or robotics planning. Neither downstream application has quantitative success measurements or comparative evaluation.

Some reporting inconsistencies affect reproducibility and interpretation. Section 4.3 specifies every fifth selected block, while Appendix A.1 specifies every third block, matching the seven-block ablation. Additionally, the claim of uncompromised video quality overlooks motion smoothness dropping from 0.990 for the data-matched baseline to 0.937, despite similar aggregate scores.

strengths: Addresses a useful control problem: specifying the object an actor should interact with using only an initial-frame mask and an action prompt, without requiring motion trajectories.

Substantial improvements over the same-data fine-tuned baseline: Contact Score increases from 0.638 to 0.878 and human-rated interaction accuracy from 0.596 to 0.892. Human preferences and stricter temporal/contact-plus-motion metrics corroborate the gains.

Convincing ablations support the central mechanism: mask conditioning alone achieves 0.647 Contact Score, while adding attention supervision raises it to 0.878. Additional experiments examine supervision regions, block selection, captions, and mask robustness.

The approach is practical, with a relatively small curated dataset, LoRA training, and detailed training settings. Qualitative demonstrations suggest useful transfer to non-human actors and complex scenes.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the method combines mask-channel conditioning, a designated text token, and attention-map supervision. Comparisons primarily involve one backbone and an adapted attention-modulation baseline; broader comparisons with spatial grounding approaches would strengthen the contribution.

Evaluation covers only 80 images, with insufficient documentation of image provenance, scene diversity, and separation from training data. Confidence intervals and uncertainty across training runs are absent, limiting interpretation of smaller ablation differences.

Contact metrics compare detections against the initial target mask rather than tracking target identity throughout the interaction. Even the extended metrics do not establish completion of the requested action or physical correctness. Human evaluations mitigate this concern but primarily assess target alignment.

The physical HOI and motion-planning claims exceed the downstream evidence. Appendix A.2 disables object-motion modules and manually aligns simulated human motions with scenes; no quantitative object-interaction success or physical-validity evaluation is provided.
The claim of uncompromised video quality needs qualification: motion smoothness decreases from 0.990 for the same-data baseline to 0.937, despite similar aggregate scores.

Some implementation details are inconsistent: Section 4.3 specifies every fifth selected transformer block, whereas Appendix A.1 specifies every third. The attention-modulation discussion also claims consistently worse performance than vanilla CogVideoX, although several Table 10 settings exceed its reported score.
